name: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
title: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
answer: Weekly updates are short, specific messages sent to parents about their child's missed assignments, grades, and attendance while there is still time to act. They matter because parents often learn how a child is doing only when a report card arrives, which is too late to help, and the trials described found that these updates reduced course failures and raised attendance and math scores.

sections.body: Many parents do not find out how their child is doing until a report card comes home, and by that point it is often too late to change anything. Weekly updates solve this by giving families concrete information about missed work, grades, and absences while the term is still running. The messages are short, specific, and frequent, so they are easy to read and easy to act on. The point is not to send more communication in general but to send the particular facts that let a parent step in and help. This turns a report card from a verdict into a warning that arrives in time.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In middle and high schools, the weekly messages described cover missed assignments, grades, and absences, and they go out often enough to keep parents current. In low income schools in Chile, the weekly messages covered attendance, grades, and behavior. The text does not separate these practices by elementary grade band, so the pattern it gives is a weekly rhythm of short, specific alerts rather than a single long report. A teacher can use AI to draft short weekly summaries for a class, then personalize each one with the student's missing work and grades from the gradebook. Tools such as TalkingPoints can send the messages in families' languages, and the teacher reviews the messages before they go out.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this evidence as coming from randomized trials. In a randomized trial in middle and high schools, weekly automated text messages to parents about missed assignments, grades, and absences cut course failures by 27 percent and raised class attendance by 12 percent (Bergman et al., 2021). A trial in low income schools in Chile found similar benefits: weekly text messages to parents about attendance, grades, and behavior raised math scores by 0.09 standard deviations (Berlinski et al., 2021). The messages cost very little to send and worked by giving parents information they could act on. The evidence is for specific kinds of alerts, not for any message a school might send, and general newsletters are useful but are not what the trials tested.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The evidence covers specific alerts, not every message a school might send, so a weekly newsletter is not the same thing as a weekly update about a missed assignment or a low grade. The information has to be concrete and it has to arrive while there is still time for a parent to act. AI can draft the summaries, but the teacher personalizes them with each student's missing work and grades from the gradebook, and the teacher reviews the messages before they go out. The decisions about what to send, what a message says about a child, and whether it is accurate stay with the teacher and the school. This is a description of practice, not legal advice.
